sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section discusses the grammatical and conceptual difficulties in the verse about Yaakov's stone, questioning how a stone can add perfection to G-d.

translations.translation: Now, in the weekly Torah portion
(Parshat Vayeitzei4)
it is stated5
“And this stone, which I have set as a pillar, shall be a house of G-d,” etc.
That which is said, “And this stone,” refers to what was stated before this6
“And he took the stone that he had placed at his head, and set it as a pillar, and poured oil on its top.”
And the grammatical difficulties in this are known
(and also see the discourse of the Baal HaHilula beginning “Vayidar Yaakov neder” in Torat Chaim7),
[regarding] what is the novelty and elevation in this—that he set the stone as a pillar and that he poured oil on its top.
Also, one must understand what is stated8
“And Yaakov vowed a vow, saying, ‘If… and this stone, which I have set as a pillar, shall be a house of G-d,’”
meaning that when all the conditions enumerated before this are fulfilled—that G-d will be with me, etc.—
then, specifically then, the stone will be a house of G-d,
that in addition to the elevation from the stones of the place
(plural)
becoming one stone9,
and in addition to the elevation of “and he set it as a pillar” and the elevation of “and he poured oil on its top,”
behold, in addition to all the above elevations,
there will be a greater elevation in the stone,
that it will be a house of G-d.
Now, the explanation of “And this stone… shall be a house of G-d” is,
that just as a house in its simple sense adds elevation and perfection to the person who dwells in the house
(as explained in many discourses,
and particularly in the discourses that explain the matter of the Holy Temple,
the discourse beginning “Mizmor shir chanukat habayit l’Dovid”10),
so too, “this stone” etc. will add elevation and perfection, so to speak, in G-d.
And one must understand,
how is it possible that a stone should add elevation in G-d?
Now, since “And this stone… shall be a house of G-d” comes in continuation of what was stated before this11
“And Havayah will be to me for a G-d,”
it is understood
that the intention is that the stone will be a house
(not for the aspect of Elokim in general,
but rather)
for the aspect of Elokim,
just as Havayah will be for a G-d.
That is, the stone will add perfection also in the aspect of Havayah that will be for a G-d.
And also, one must understand
(as is asked in Torat Chaim there)
that which is stated “And this stone” in the feminine,
and afterwards “shall be a house,” etc.,
for it should have said “shall be a house,” etc., in the feminine,
and if “stone” is masculine,
it should have said “this stone” in the masculine, etc.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section connects the redemption of Yud Tes Kislev and Yud Kislev to the verse “He redeemed my soul in peace,” explaining its relevance through the monthly and weekly Tehillim cycles.

translations.translation: Now, the day of the Hilula
(9 Kislev)
is the eve of the day of redemption12
(10 Kislev13).
And it is known that redemption is related to the matter of “He redeemed my soul in peace”14,
as stated by the Rebbe, the Alter Rebbe, in his holy letter15
(regarding the redemption of Yud Tes Kislev)
“When I called out… ‘He redeemed my soul in peace’… I came out in peace.”
From this it is understood16
also regarding the redemption of the Rebbe, the Mitteler Rebbe17,
that the redemption is related to the matter of “He redeemed my soul in peace,” which is recited in the monthly portion of Tehillim
(on the tenth day of the month).
And particularly according to what is known18,
that the established order among our holy Rebbes and Nesi’im was that they would recite the portion of Tehillim as divided according to the days of the month,
and at certain times they would recite Tehillim at length19,
meaning they would add and also recite the weekly portion of Tehillim—through which the Rebbe, my father-in-law, the Rebbe13 explains
that which the Alter Rebbe said on Yud Tes Kislev, the verse “He redeemed my soul in peace,”
even though this verse is not in the monthly portion of the 19th day of the month, but rather in the Tehillim chapters of the third day of the week
(and Yud Tes Kislev fell then on the third day),
because when the Alter Rebbe was imprisoned, he added and also recited the weekly portion of Tehillim.
Behold, from this the connection of the redemption to the matter of “He redeemed my soul in peace” is even more understood.
For the fixed portion is the monthly portion of Tehillim,
and the portion of the 19th day of the month is “Tefilah l’Moshe,”
which also relates to the redemption20,
and nevertheless the Alter Rebbe connects his redemption specifically to the verse “He redeemed my soul in peace,”
behold, this compels even more the connection of the matter of redemption to this verse.
And from this it is understood that this is also the case regarding the redemption of Yud Kislev,
as above.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains that the novelty of the verse “He redeemed my soul in peace” is that the redemption was through peace, not war, because even those who were “many” were with him.

translations.translation: And the matter is,
that the main novelty in the verse “He redeemed my soul in peace” is
(not the essence of the redemption itself,
but rather as the Baal HaHilula explains in the discourse beginning “Pidah b’shalom nafshi”21
(in his book Shaarei Teshuvah))
in this—that the redemption is in peace.
For it is possible for redemption to be through war,
and the novelty in this redemption is that
(even though it is from those close to me,
nevertheless)
“He redeemed in peace”
(specifically)
“my soul.”
And this is also the explanation of the continuation of the verse, “for many were with me,”
for the word “for” provides a reason for the beginning of his statement, “He redeemed my soul in peace,”
that the reason He redeemed specifically in peace and not through war is—that “many were with me”22.
For through this, that even those who are of the aspect of “many” were with me23,
in the manner of the saying of our Rabbis, of blessed memory24,
that even the men of Avshalom prayed for Dovid,
behold, through this “He redeemed my soul in peace.”
